facts: Satellite clocks gain about 45 µs a day from weaker gravity (general relativity) and lose about 7 µs a day from their speed (special relativity). The net is +38 µs a day, which would make your position drift about 10 km a day if nobody corrected it.
The fix is built in before launch: GPS clocks are tuned to 10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz, so they tick at the right rate once they're in orbit.
Light covers about 30 cm per nanosecond. A clock error of just 1 µs puts you about 300 m off.
Your phone needs 4 satellites, not 3. The fourth solves your phone's own cheap clock error, so for a moment your phone keeps time almost as well as an atomic clock.
A GPS signal reaches you weaker than the background radio noise (around -130 dBm). The receiver digs it out by correlating with a known code, which is also why a small jammer can drown it out.
GPS time started on 6 January 1980 and never adds leap seconds. Today it runs 18 seconds ahead of UTC.
The old GPS message counts weeks with only 10 bits, so the count rolls over to 0 every 1024 weeks. That happened in August 1999 and April 2019, and some old receivers jumped back 20 years.
